Journey doc corroborates in his own words (line 488): "decomposing the existing monolith into microservices by defining the boundaries", and the doc calls it "your *first* monolith-to-microservices decomposition, which makes it load-bearing for every architect interview."

Deque (résumé): "Championed decomposition of a monolith into **10–15 services**, splitting on independent scaling and database ownership rather than on team boundaries". Journey doc line 600 gives the rule verbatim: "a component became a microservice if it needed to scale independently or needed its own database. Each service owned its database; each database was multi-tenant."

The stronger-than-decomposition claim, journey doc line 198: "This was not one monolith split into pieces. Authentication was its own service in Java and Spring Boot, serving every product in the portfolio… Billing and subscription was a second cross-product service… Global configuration was a third. Ten to fifteen services by the time I left." The doc's own note (line 572): "the services you built were *cross-product platform services*, not just a decomposition of one application. A billing service consumed by every product in the portfolio is a materially stronger claim than 'we split the monolith.'"

SOLUTION ARCHITECTURE / DESIGN TRADE-OFFS — the JD asks for "Strong expertise in System Design and Solution Architecture". Journey doc line 597 records an evaluated trade-off with a chosen option and a reason: "Two options were evaluated: one database per customer, or a tenant/organisation-ID column on every table… Chosen: **organisation ID on every table**, with the tenant resolved from the **JWT** on every incoming request, so a single codebase served both models — no forked microservice versions." Plus the distinction that makes it architecture rather than plumbing (line 190): "The banks that would not share infrastructure kept their own database — against that same code. That is a deployment difference, not a second codebase, and holding that line is what kept it maintainable."

DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS / SCALABILITY PATTERNS — the JD's "Design systems handling high traffic, high concurrency, large-scale workloads". Journey doc line 649: "a single message will result in 50 external calls", corroborated by code not memory (line 651): "`GROUNDING.md` counts roughly **48–58 external calls per message, of which 13–23 are OpenSearch calls**… The 50 figure is accurate and if anything conservative." Résumé: "Stewarded a **zero-downtime** upgrade from **PostgreSQL 9.6** to **Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL 13.x** across every axe Auditor instance".

scores.verdict:
9/10 — this is his strongest criterion, and it is the one the JD weights heaviest. Do not discount it.

The JD's Naukri skill tags are literally "System Design, Distribution System, Java, High Level Design, System Architecture", and its core ask is "Design and oversee architecture for scalable, distributed, microservices-based systems". Against that, he brings three monolith decompositions across three employers, two in Java and Spring Boot, plus the thing that separates an architect from an engineer who split a monolith: a stated, defensible boundary rule — "it earns its own process if it needs to scale independently or needs to own its data" — and cross-product platform services (auth, billing/subscription, global config) consumed by every product in a portfolio. That is a stronger microservices claim than the JD asks for.

Solution architecture is evidenced the way a panel actually tests it — as an evaluated trade-off with a chosen option and a reason. DB-per-customer versus org-ID-on-every-table, chosen deliberately, tenant resolved from the JWT, one code path, and the banks that refused shared infrastructure kept their own database against that same code because "that is a deployment difference, not a second codebase". Distributed systems is evidenced by a fan-out problem stated in nine words and corroborated by code rather than memory (48–58 external calls per message), a Go rewrite, a two-stream Kinesis design built explicitly for spike headroom, and an event-sourced DynamoDB single-table with CQRS and a deterministic snapshot exporter. Caching, async, messaging and event-driven — one full JD sub-block — is covered three times over across three eras, including a deliberate decision NOT to add Redis to a query path, which is the kind of answer that wins design rounds. Resiliency is not hand-waved: circuit breakers with a stated budget ("circuit breaker at 1.5s — defer panel · never block warm path"), per-tenant and per-role rate limits, idempotent resumable backfills, all in shipped code.

Two JD required sub-lines are only partly met — high availability designed against failure, and load balancing. Both are absent from the written record rather than contradicted by it, and one of them (load balancing) is almost certainly a documentation gap in the journey doc rather than a real one. The concurrency headline is a burst test and the two-stream design was never load-tested, both by his own admission. Those cost the tenth point. They do not cost more than that, because 19 years of "I get handed systems that work but can no longer scale the way they are built" is exactly the sentence this seat is buying, and because his zero-downtime record across ~300 instances is a harder availability skill than most candidates who can quote a nines figure actually possess.

Smallest honest lift for this criterion — all Rule 7 re-vectoring of real work, no new claims:
- Lead the VoltusWave block with the fan-out number, not the Kinesis shard count. "A single patient message fanned out into ~50 downstream calls" is the sentence that makes every follow-up write itself, and it is corroborated in code.
- Re-vector the Deque block to foreground the 10–15 services and the boundary rule ahead of the tenancy mechanics — the JD asks for microservices architecture first and multi-tenancy not at all.

| Loss | Points | Recoverable? |

Writing any of those is the cardinal sin. **An honest 88 that survives the room beats a fabricated 95 that does not.**

## 2. THE BINDING CONSTRAINT

**The résumé does not currently read as a Java architect's résumé — and underneath that, his last hands-on Java seat ended February 2025.**

That is the largest single weighted loss (4.0 of the 17), and it splits cleanly. The unfixable half is time: fourteen months of Python, FastAPI, LangChain and Go against a JD whose first two required lines are "Strong hands-on experience with **Java**" and "Strong expertise in **Spring Boot**". The fixable half is placement: the Deque block opens on multi-tenancy and never names Java until bullet three, the Engineering Excellence block runs six AI-methodology lines through its middle, and **El Paso prints as .NET on the live card — hiding four of the eleven Java years on a Java-first JD.**

The hard floor underneath it is **Kubernetes** — the only genuinely required technology absent without trace, worth 2.25 points that no edit closes. It is a floor, not the constraint: the JD's verb there is "Experience with", the weakest phrasing in its entire required block, against "Strong hands-on" for Java and "Extensive" for microservices.

## 3. THE SMALLEST HONEST LIFT

Est. +5 to +6 points, all Rule 7 re-vectoring of real work. **Zero new claims.**

**A. Reorder, don't rewrite — highest yield, no honesty cost**

1. **`quick-deque` — lead with Java.** Order for this seat: `Forged a central authentication service in **Java and Spring Boot**…` → `Productized a billing and subscription service… porting it from **Node.js/TypeScript** to **Java and Spring Boot**` → `Championed decomposition of a monolith into **10–15 services**, splitting on independent scaling and database ownership` → then the tenancy bullets. Why: the JD asks for Java, Spring Boot and microservices in that order and never asks for multi-tenancy at all. Today a Java reader hits two tenancy bullets before the word "Java" appears.
2. **`quick-skills-ee` — promote three lines, demote four.** Move `Java + Spring Boot Microservices`, `System Design at Scale` and `Cloud Infrastructure & Platform Engineering (AWS…)` to positions 1–3. For this seat drop `Statistical Rigor in Production AI`, `Leakage-Safe Machine Learning`, `LLM Productionisation` and `Self-Hosted Models In-VPC` — they buy nothing at a beauty-and-wellness marketplace and VoltusWave's 10 bullets will not fit three pages regardless.
3. **`quick-voltuswave` — lead with the fan-out, trim the clinic.** Keep Kinesis/Go/Datadog first; cut `Extracted confounder-gated cohort comparisons…` and `Sequenced patient event histories…` for this job only. Per-job trim, never a master edit.
4. **Headline** — consider swapping `Neptune + GNN · LLM` for a microservices/AWS phrase for this seat. `Java + Spring Boot` is already in word-position four, which is right.

**B. Three bullets that close four required JD lines, all sourced**

- **VoltusWave, CI/CD + containers** (closes the two weakest required lines at once): `Spearheaded a containerized deployment pipeline, cutting infrastructure cost **25–30%** and deploy time from hours to **under 10 minutes**` — 19 words, both facts user-confirmed 2026-08-25, verb free, current role only. Also add **Docker** explicitly beside ECS in the skills cloud line (docker compose at Deque is in his own handwriting). *Do not name ECS or EKS on the 2025–26 stint — that platform is undocumented. Ask him; if he names it, add it.*

Takes observability from one startup to a multi-hundred-instance portfolio.
- **VoltusWave, resiliency + caching**: `Strengthened serving-path resiliency with per-tenant namespaced **Redis** caches at a **6-hour** time-to-live, request coalescing, circuit breakers and per-role rate limits` — all from his own KQ4/KQ9/KQ10 documents. **D. Ask him one question before drafting:** what index design backed the org-ID predicate across ~300 instances, and what changed on the 9.6 → Aurora 13.x jump? One confirmed bullet closes the recent-indexing gap. Do not draft it until he answers.

## 4. REAL-WORLD GATES — named separately, dragging neither score

**COMPENSATION — the hardest gate, and it should be tested before any interview cycle is spent.** The band is ₹60–80L. **Its midpoint, ₹70L, is ₹2L below what he earns today.** To clear his ₹75L floor he has to land at the **75th percentile of a band written for a 12-year architect while bringing 19+ years**, and the best realistic outcome — ₹80L, their ceiling — is an 11% step with zero headroom left for negotiation afterwards. **₹1Cr is 25% above their maximum and is not on this table.** Per the standing rule: quote ₹75L–₹1Cr fixed, anchored to the seat's level rather than to him, and do not volunteer ₹72L. Treat the band as a qualifying question on the first call, not a closing one.

**LOCATION — Sector 63, Noida, explicitly Work From Office.** He is in Hyderabad. Relocation is open and is **not** a scoring constraint. But this is not a foreign-city timezone anchor with a remote read available — a named sector plus WFO means a real move. And it compounds the gate above: a household relocation funded out of a band whose midpoint is below his current salary. Worth asking on the call whether any hybrid exists.

**LEVELLING — good shape, wrong price point.** "Lead Architect" is genuinely IC: mentor senior engineers and tech leads, lead architectural reviews, no people-management mandate. That is exactly the seat type v2 exists to pursue and the fit is strong (9/10). But they asked for 12+ and he brings 19+, having been Co-Founder and VP of Technology — two title steps above. Expect the overqualification and flight-risk read; he has the answer prepared already (journey l.263: *"the architect seat is the one I actually want"*). The band is the tell: they are pricing a 12–15-year architect.

**LEGITIMACY — 3.9 over 185 reviews.** Directionally fine for Indian consumer tech, but 185 is a thin sample — enough to read, not enough to decide on. The research pass must (a) verify the seat is actually open on the company's own careers page and whether it is a new headcount or a backfill, (b) check whether an architect layer already exists or he would be the first, and (c) check the company's public news cycle for the widely-reported employee-communications controversy and how it was resolved — culture diligence, surfaced for his judgement, not a recommendation.

## 5. WHAT TO EXPECT IN THE ROOM

**1. "What's your Kubernetes experience — how would you run this on K8s?"** Guaranteed: it is required, it is absent, and it is the one gap an architecture panel can test in five minutes. He must map ECS to K8s vocabulary out loud and unprompted — task definition → Pod spec / Deployment, ECS service → ReplicaSet, ALB target group → Service + Ingress, target-tracking scaling → HPA, Fargate → managed node pool — then say plainly that he has architected on ECS and has not run Kubernetes in production. **Claiming it in the room is the one move that turns a survivable gap into a rejection.** Route as a named drill to `~/Documents/interview-prep/`.

**2. "Which Spring Boot version, and when did you last write Java?"** Guaranteed by a JD that opens on hands-on Java. The honest answers are Spring Boot **2.x**, Java **8/17**, and February 2025. He should volunteer the 2.x → 3.x delta himself — javax → jakarta namespace migration, the new observability stack, native images — and note he has run harder migrations than that (Keycloak → Red Hat SSO across ~300 instances, PostgreSQL 9.6 → Aurora 13.x zero-downtime). Volunteering the delta is what makes it read as currency rather than drift.

**3. "A hundred thousand concurrent — what did it hold in production?"** Guaranteed at a consumer marketplace. The honest answer is that it was a **burst test — one request per user, no sustained load, no 500-user baseline** — and that the two-stream Kinesis design was never limit-tested because the budget never came. Lead with the problem, not the number: *"a single message fanned out into about fifty downstream calls"* (corroborated in code at 48–58). Volunteer the burst caveat before it is extracted. **The résumé wording stays exactly as written — it is on the open confirm-or-reject list and it is his call alone.**
